title: EMF and Internal Resistance
notes: **EMF ($\\\\mathcal{E}$):** the open-circuit voltage of a source. It is the work done per unit charge in moving charge around the complete circuit.
**Internal resistance $r$:** the resistance inside the cell due to electrolyte and electrodes. It causes the terminal voltage to drop when current flows.
**Terminal voltage:** $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$. When no current flows ($I=0$), $V = \\\\mathcal{E}$. Under load, $V < \\\\mathcal{E}$.
**Cells in series:** $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = \\\\mathcal{E}_1 + \\\\mathcal{E}_2 + \\\\ldots$, $r_{total} = r_1 + r_2 + \\\\ldots$. Series adds both EMF and internal resistance.
**Cells in parallel:** $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = \\\\mathcal{E}$ (if all equal), $r_{total} = r/n$ for $n$ identical cells. Parallel reduces internal resistance, allowing higher current delivery.
**Maximum power transfer:** the power delivered to an external load $R$ is maximum when $R = r$. The maximum power is $P_{max} = \\\\mathcal{E}^2/(4r)$.
**Current in a simple circuit:** $I = \\\\mathcal{E}/(R + r)$, where $R$ is the external resistance and $r$ is the internal resistance.
**Efficiency:** the efficiency of power transfer is $\\\\eta = R/(R + r)$. Maximum efficiency approaches 100% when $R \\\\gg r$, but maximum power requires $R = r$.
**Short circuit current:** when $R = 0$, $I_{sc} = \\\\mathcal{E}/r$. This can be very large and dangerous, causing heating and damage.
**Cells with different EMFs:** when cells with different EMFs are connected in parallel, circulating currents flow between them. This can damage cells and should be avoided.
**Real cell behavior:** as a cell discharges, its EMF slowly decreases and its internal resistance increases. An old battery reads lower than its rated voltage even when not loaded.
confusion: EMF is not a force - it is a voltage (energy per unit charge). The name is historical. EMF is measured in volts, not newtons.

Terminal voltage $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$ is less than EMF when current flows out of the cell. But when charging the cell, current flows into the positive terminal, so $V = \\\\mathcal{E} + Ir$ - the terminal voltage is greater than EMF.
In series, both EMF and internal resistance add. In parallel, the equivalent EMF is the same as one cell, but the equivalent internal resistance is reduced, allowing more current.
Maximum power transfer ($R = r$) occurs at 50% efficiency. For efficient power delivery, you want $R \\\\gg r$ (high efficiency, low power). For maximum power, you sacrifice efficiency.
A fresh battery has a high open-circuit voltage (close to its EMF) but drops significantly under load if its internal resistance has increased with age. That is why old batteries seem weak.
practice: A cell with EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 $\\\Omega$ is connected to a 7 $\\\Omega$ resistor. Find the current, terminal voltage, and power delivered to the resistor. Solution: $I = 1.5/(7+0.5) = 0.2$ A. $V = 1.5 - 0.2 \	imes 0.5 = 1.4$ V. $P = I^2 R = 0.04 \	imes 7 = 0.28$ W.

A cell gives 2.0 V when no current flows and 1.8 V when delivering 1 A. Find the EMF and internal resistance. Solution: EMF $\\\\mathcal{E} = 2.0$ V (open circuit). Under load: $1.8 = 2.0 - 1 \	imes r$, so $r = 0.2\\\\,\\\\Omega$.

Three identical cells of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.3 $\\\Omega$ each are connected in series across a 6 $\\\Omega$ load. Find the current. Solution: $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = 4.5$ V, $r_{total} = 0.9\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $I = 4.5/(6+0.9) = 0.652$ A.

The same three cells above are connected in parallel across the same 6 $\\\Omega$ load. Find the current. Solution: $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = 1.5$ V, $r_{total} = 0.3/3 = 0.1\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $I = 1.5/(6+0.1) = 0.246$ A.

Find the external resistance for maximum power transfer to a cell with EMF 12 V and internal resistance 2 $\\\Omega$. Find the maximum power. Solution: $R = r = 2\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $I = 12/(2+2) = 3$ A. $P_{max} = I^2 R = 9 \	imes 2 = 18$ W. Alternatively $P_{max} = \\\\mathcal{E}^2/(4r) = 144/8 = 18$ W.
universalFacts: The internal resistance of a typical AA alkaline cell is about 0.15 $\\\Omega$ when fresh, but increases to 0.5 $\\\Omega$ or more as it discharges.
Connecting cells in series increases the available voltage while keeping the same current capacity. Connecting in parallel increases the current capacity while keeping the same voltage.
A short-circuited 12 V car battery with internal resistance 0.01 $\\\Omega$ can deliver 1200 A, which is why it can melt tools and cause severe burns.
The maximum power transfer theorem ($R = r$) is a fundamental design principle for matching loads to sources, but it is inefficient for power distribution systems where $R \\\\gg r$ is desired.
In a battery pack, series strings are often used to increase voltage, and parallel strings within each series group are used to increase capacity and reduce internal resistance.
summary: The electromotive force ℰ of a source is its open-circuit voltage, that is the work done per unit charge in moving charge around the complete circuit, and it is measured in volts rather than newtons despite the historical name. Every real cell also has an internal resistance r arising from its electrolyte and electrodes, so the terminal voltage under load is V = ℰ − Ir, which equals ℰ only when no current flows. The current in a simple circuit is therefore I = ℰ/(R + r), with R the external resistance. Cells in series add both their emf and their internal resistance, whereas cells in parallel leave the equivalent emf unchanged at ℰ while reducing the internal resistance to r/n for n identical cells, which allows a much larger current to be delivered. The power delivered to a load R is greatest when R = r, giving P_max = ℰ²/(4r).
importantConcepts: EMF ℰ defined as the open-circuit voltage of the source, equal to the work done per unit charge around the circuit.
Internal resistance r due to the electrolyte and the electrodes, which is why the terminal voltage falls when current flows.
Terminal voltage V = ℰ − Ir when the cell discharges, reducing to V = ℰ at zero current.
Current in a single loop I = ℰ/(R + r), in which the internal resistance appears in series with the external resistance.
Series combination adding both emf and internal resistance, against parallel combination which keeps ℰ and divides r by n.
Maximum power transfer to the load when R = r, giving a maximum power of ℰ²/(4r).
importantStatements: The emf of a cell is the potential difference across its terminals when no current is drawn from it.
The terminal voltage of a discharging cell is less than its emf and is given by V = ℰ − Ir.
When cells are connected in series their emfs and their internal resistances both add.
When identical cells are connected in parallel the equivalent emf is unchanged and the internal resistance becomes r/n.
The power delivered to an external resistance is maximum when the external resistance equals the internal resistance.
importantTasks: Find the current, terminal voltage and power delivered in a circuit containing a cell of emf ℰ, internal resistance r and load R.
Determine the emf and internal resistance of a cell from its open-circuit voltage and its voltage under a known load.
Combine several cells in series and in parallel, stating both the equivalent emf and the equivalent internal resistance.
Show that the power delivered to the load is maximum when R = r and evaluate that maximum power.
keyPoints: Always include r in the total resistance: I = ℰ/(R + r), never I = ℰ/R for a real cell.
EMF is a voltage measured in volts, not a force, so it is energy per unit charge.
Series raises the emf but also raises the internal resistance; parallel lowers the internal resistance to deliver more current.
The open-circuit voltage of a cell is its emf, which is how a voltmeter of very high resistance measures it.
Maximum power transfer at R = r is the condition for a source delivering the most power to a load, not for a source being most efficient.
specialNotes: EMF is a voltage, that is energy per unit charge, measured in volts and not in newtons; the name is purely historical.
While the cell discharges, V = ℰ − Ir, but while it is being charged the current enters the positive terminal and the terminal voltage rises to V = ℰ + Ir.
In series both the emf and the internal resistance add, whereas in parallel the emf is unchanged and only the internal resistance is reduced, so parallel cells can deliver far more current.
Open-circuit voltage equals emf only because no current flows, so a voltmeter must have a very high resistance for the reading to be trustworthy.
Maximum power transfer at R = r wastes half the available energy as heat inside the cell, so it is not the condition of maximum efficiency.
examShortTricks: Put the internal resistance in series with the external one the moment you see a cell, so the total is R + r before any other step.
A cell that reads 2.0 V open circuit and 1.8 V at 1 A has r = 0.2 Ω by simple subtraction, which settles a two mark question instantly.
For n identical cells in parallel, the internal resistance is r/n but the emf stays ℰ; in series the emf is nℰ and the resistance is nr.
Write the terminal voltage as V = ℰ − Ir and remember that the drop across the internal resistance is exactly the loss I²r in power.
examNotes: A three mark numerical giving ℰ, r and R and asking for the current, terminal voltage and power in the resistor is extremely common.
A two mark item asks for the emf and internal resistance from an open-circuit and a loaded voltage reading.
Series and parallel combinations of cells are a regular four or five mark question requiring both the equivalent emf and the equivalent internal resistance.
One mark questions test the definition of emf as the open-circuit voltage, and frequently the fact that it is measured in volts.
